content: 1. The mechanisms of medicine delivery should be tailored to contexts where their effectiveness has been proven, ensuring optimal therapeutic outcomes. 2. In the domain of sexual health, it is essential to enhance access to condoms and lubricants by utilizing diverse distribution outlets to promote safer sexual practices. 3. Menstrual products must be prioritized as essential health items, and their inclusion in priority health product lists is critical to prevent supply chain disruptions. 4. Communication strategies should emphasize the availability and benefits of alternative, reusable menstrual health products to ensure sustainable options for users. 5. Community groups, where available, should be engaged to expand the accessibility of menstrual products, particularly in underserved areas. 6. The availability of self-testing kits for HIV and self-collection tools for sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including syphilis, should be increased. These tools should be accompanied by clear referral pathways to treatment when necessary. 7. Messaging around safe and consensual sexual practices during periods of self-isolation should be prioritized, particularly for individuals receiving HIV medications, undergoing menopause management, or engaging in gender-affirming hormonal therapy. 8. For cervical cancer prevention, self-sampling for HPV testing should be promoted, with specimen collection facilitated through pharmacies or drop-off points at healthcare facilities. 9. Online platforms should provide advice following negative screening tests and ensure adequate management and follow-up for individuals with positive screening results. 10. In managing non-communicable diseases, self-management plans should be developed and supported by healthcare workers. These plans should include self-monitoring of conditions and alternative delivery mechanisms for care when necessary. 11. Home supplies of medications and monitoring devices should be increased to enable individuals to manage acute exacerbations of conditions, such as short courses of steroids, at home under a clinician-approved self-management plan. 12. For diabetes management, individuals with type 1 diabetes should be provided with urine ketone self-monitoring strips and have access to phone consultations with healthcare providers. 13. During pandemics, digital technologies and platforms play a crucial role in maintaining access to reproductive health interventions, services, and treatments when traditional healthcare access points are limited. 14. Over-the-counter availability of medical devices, medicines, and diagnostics should be expanded globally. Examples include oral contraceptives, menstrual hygiene products, and post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV, particularly for individuals at increased risk of sexual violence. 15. Legal reforms, such as decriminalizing consensual sexual behaviors and recognizing the legal gender of transgender individuals, are critical to creating a supportive environment for underserved and marginalized populations. 16. Transgender and gender-diverse individuals who self-administer gender-affirming hormones require access to evidence-based information, high-quality products, and sterile injection equipment. Healthcare systems should also provide support for managing adverse events and offer other gender-affirmative care options. 17. Efforts to reduce stigma and discrimination at the national level, including anti-discrimination laws and protective policies, are essential to fostering a supportive environment for underserved populations, particularly within healthcare and justice systems. 18. A life-course approach to health recognizes the interconnected roles of individual, intergenerational, social, environmental, and temporal factors in shaping health and well-being. This approach emphasizes timely interventions at key life stages to address the root causes of disease and ill health. 19. Age-appropriate environments and policies that reduce ageism are integral to addressing the health needs of populations across the age spectrum. This includes fostering age-friendly environments as part of global strategies on aging and health. 20. Sexual health remains a critical consideration for older adults. A life-course approach that is sensitive, respectful, and informed about the unique challenges and opportunities at all ages can help reduce age-based discrimination and stereotypes. 21. Improving health literacy among older adults regarding accurate information, services, and self-care for sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) is vital to supporting informed choices and promoting well-being. 22. Legal and policy reforms aligned with international human rights standards are necessary to protect the health and rights of underserved and marginalized populations. Without such measures, barriers to accessing essential health services, including self-care interventions, will persist. 23. Harm-reduction campaigns, such as those addressing the use of psychoactive prescription drugs among youth, should provide accurate information and support safe practices to mitigate risks associated with misuse.
